 EXAMINING HOPKINS HOSPITAL'S RELATIONSHIP WITH BALTIMORE 
 A history of Indigenous Peoples' Day and Baltimore
 By JOE VATNER 
 | October 22, 2026
 COURTESY OF JOE VATNER
 The site of Baltimore’s toppled Christopher Columbus statue. 
 On Monday, Oct. 12 the University and the city of Baltimore celebrated Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Simultaneously, Maryland and the U.S. federal government celebrated Columbus Day. 
 The name of the second Monday of October has been a national debate for decades. In some states, both names are listed, while other states choose just one. The federal government gives its employees a paid day off for Columbus Day, but some states regard Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a “ public holiday ” without the day off for state government employees. Maryland is unique in that there is both a paid state holiday for Columbus Day and American Indian Heritage Day, the Friday after Thanksgiving.
 Different groups have differing opinions on Maryland’s and Baltimore’s choices of days of celebration. In a written interview with The News-Letter , Nina Gover Brooks, the director of the Baltimore American Indian Center (BAIC) shared her perspective on the debate.
 “Indigenous People's Day should be considered and recognized as a state holiday,” she explained. “Although we are excited to hear about the announcement of American Indian Heritage Day, many people feel it makes indigenous people seem like an afterthought…greatly overshadowed by the American celebration of Thanksgiving and Black Friday given the fact that is the Friday after the major holiday,“ she wrote. 
 The News-Letter also reached out to John Pica, the Baltimore-based President of Italian American Organizations United, who shared his thoughts in an interview with The News-Letter . Pica’s response to Baltimore’s decision to rename Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples’ Day was generally supportive. 
 “We had no problem with renaming Columbus Day to Italian Heritage Day, but the council wouldn't do that, so Indigenous Peoples Day is fine, and we don't oppose that at all,” he said. “In Baltimore City, it really doesn't matter what they do, because it's not recognized as officially changing the holiday. There's still a federal holiday, and there's still a state holiday.”
 To understand these differing perspectives, we must look into Baltimore’s complicated history of the holiday. 
 History 
 Baltimore was one of the first cities to celebrate Columbus Day. On Oct. 12, 1792 the Columbus Obelisk was erected in Baltimore, celebrating the 300th anniversary of Columbus’ landing. Since then, Baltimore has put up two more statues honoring Columbus, one in Druid Hill Park and one in the appropriately named Columbus Park, adjacent to Baltimore’s Little Italy neighborhood. The last one was torn down in 2020 .
 The city’s large Italian community, centered around the historic St. Leo’s Catholic Church, celebrated the holiday with a parade for 122 years, the longest running Columbus parade in the country. This is much longer than the day has even existed as a federal holiday. Columbus Day was only designated as a federal holiday in 1968 , during the Lyndon B. Johnson administration. 
 For centuries, Christopher Columbus was treated as a hero and as the “ discoverer of the Americas ” by American schools. His journey has been a symbolic source of pride for Italian American communities, who have faced xenophobic discrimination in the history of the U.S. However, through the consistent efforts of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous historians and scholars, the heroic perception of Columbus as a person has shifted. His actions have been critically reexamined, and it is generally agreed that he perpetrated the conquest, enslavement and murder of Indigenous people. Furthermore, his actions, the intentionality of which remains debated, led to the genocide of the Indigenous population of the Americas: it is estimated that 95% of the Indigenous population of the Americas died in the 130 years after 1492. 
 In 1977 , not long after Columbus Day’s designation as a federal holiday, groups began advocating for its name to be changed. In 1992, Indigenous groups protested national quincentennial Columbus Day celebrations, and states and cities began changing Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples’ Day. 
 Baltimore has a rich and continuous history of Indigenous presence. Baltimore contains part of the ancestral homelands of the Piscataway and Susquehannock peoples. Both tribes still have a presence in the Baltimore community. Chief Mark Tayac, the 29th-generation hereditary chief of the Piscataway Nation, was one of the leaders present at the University’s eighth annual powwow . A powwow is a traditional Indigenous American social gathering containing dancing and singing.
 Baltimore’s current Indigenous population also contains thousands of Lumbee and Cherokee people who migrated here during the 1950s and ‘60s. They mostly settled in East Baltimore, specifically in the Upper Fells Point and Washington Hill neighborhoods. Their neighborhood became nicknamed “The Reservation.” Despite much of the community moving outside “The Reservation” in the decades since, the neighborhood is still full of history. Ashley Minner, a Lumbee community artist, has created a public memory walking tour project where one can explore the neighborhood’s history. It includes churches (such as the South Broadway Baptist Church), storefronts, restaurants, community centers (such as the BAIC) and murals (such as the Duality of Indigeneity Mural).
 Baltimore’s Indigenous community has been an active force in pushing for the renaming of Columbus Day and for the celebration of Indigenous Peoples’ Day. In 2017, Kerry Hawk Lessard, the executive director of Baltimore-based Native American Lifelines and a Shawnee nation member, released a statement in support of changing Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
 “Rejecting painful reminders of the past and instead embracing the resilience and presence of Native people is an important step in the empowerment and healing of our communities,” he wrote.
 In 2020, Baltimore’s City Council passed a bill officially changing the name of Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples’ Day, with the support of the advocacy group Indigenous Strong. 
 However, Gover Brooks says the necessary work in honoring and uplifting Indigenous communities is not complete. 
 “The city of Baltimore does a pretty decent job with celebrating and recognizing Indigenous Peoples’ Day,” she said. “However, one thing I know that could change to benefit the Indigenous community here is if the city would partner with local Indigenous organizations more often to plan celebrations and/or fundraisers to keep these cultural pillars alive,“ she wrote.
 Columbus statue 
 In 2020, the combination of the increasingly critical views of Christopher Columbus and the wave of George Floyd-inspired Black Lives Matter protests culminated in the toppling of one of the historic Columbus statues in Baltimore. On the night of July 4, 2020 a large group of protestors gathered at Columbus Park, which is right by the harbor, and pulled the Columbus statue off its pedestal and dumped it into the water.
 The toppling had mixed reactions in Maryland and Baltimore. Then-governor Larry Hogan posted a statement supporting civic engagement while discouraging vandalism.
 “While we welcome peaceful protests and constructive dialogue on whether and how to put certain monuments in context or move them to museums or storage through a legal process, lawlessness, vandalism, and destruction of public property is completely unacceptable,” he wrote. “That is the antithesis of democracy and should be condemned by everyone, regardless of their politics. Baltimore City leaders need to regain control of their own streets and immediately start making them safer." 
 Meanwhile, then-City Council President and now Mayor Brandon Scott voiced his support for the removal of the Columbus statue, but not necessarily the protestors’ methods. He additionally voiced his support for Baltimore’s Italian American community and the city’s Indigenous community and stated that he cannot “support Columbus.” 
 To understand Baltimore’s large Italian American community’s reaction to the statue’s destruction, The News-Letter asked Pica about his and the community’s views on Columbus, Columbus Day and his statue. First, Pica clarified that Baltimore’s Italian American and Catholic communities’ pride in Columbus is not in the man himself, but rather is symbolic. 
 “It's symbolic of his adventure. It's symbolic of creating an oceanic highway that brought my grandparents here and immigrants all over Europe,” he said. “We don't raise a glass to Columbus. We raise a glass to Italy and to Italian American heritage.”
 His view is that the toppling of the Columbus Statue was unfavorable and ineffective. 
 “I don’t think it was related to Floyd... It was a bunch of punks between 17 and 25 years old… thinking they were doing something courageous, thinking they were doing something good,” he claimed. “In fact, they destroyed a statue that was worth more than a half million dollars. The saddest part of that whole evening was that two dozen Baltimore police officers watched the whole thing and did nothing.”
 What will take the place of the old statue? Well, Baltimore’s Italian American community used tow trucks and rope to retrieve the sunken Columbus statue from the Inner Harbor. Then, they hired a sculptor to recreate the statue . However, this replica is not on the old pedestal in Baltimore; instead, it is sitting on display at the White House in Washington, D.C. 
 There are plans for what will take Columbus’ place in Baltimore. Pica explained some possible replacement options. 
 “We’ve now raised over $240,000 for a statue of an Italian immigrant family that will go on the pedestal where Columbus once sat,” he said. “We’re going to have three brass plaques memorializing the different cultures that live there: the African Americans who lived side by side with the Italians, Jews who lived side by side on the other side of Little Italy and the two Native American tribes that preceded everyone on that land.”
 The new statue is in the works to be completed in the winter of 2027.
 Hopkins 
 Hopkins preceded Baltimore to renaming Columbus Day as Indigenous Peoples’ Day, doing so in 2018. This came after years of gatherings and protests by the University’s Indigenous students. On Indigenous Peoples’ Day in 2018, the University’s Indigenous Students at Hopkins (ISH) group and the Office of Multicultural Affairs hosted their first official powwow celebration, an annual tradition ever since.
 Despite its official celebration of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, Hopkins’ commitment to Indigenous studies leaves room to be desired. 
 Hopkins currently does not have an Indigenous studies department or a specific professor or faculty dedicated to studying American Indigenous Studies. To resolve this, students in the Critical Diaspora Studies major have created a working group, one point of advocacy being to hire a tenured faculty member in American Indigenous Studies. 
 Critics argue that without advanced research into or undergraduate-accessible classes about American Indigenous history and culture, Hopkins fails to follow its statement on principles of diversity, equity and inclusion, which emphasizes “diverse identities, perspectives, and experiences.”
 Hopkins also has a very low number of Indigenous students. Hopkins reported that the Class of 2029 has 1.1% of students of American Indian/Alaska Native background and 0.4% of Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander background. Furthermore, the formerly active ISH undergraduate organization seems to be no longer active.
 Hopkins does have a world-renowned graduate program in Indigenous studies: the Bloomberg School of Public Health’s Center for Indigenous Health . Founded in 1991, the Center has served to promote “Indigenous health equity through evidence-based public health programs, education, innovative research, policy advocacy, and the dissemination of proven programs tailored to community needs.” While physically based in Washington, D.C., most of the work of the center takes place in actual Indigenous communities across the U.S. and the rest of the world. 80% of the Center’s employees are Indigenous, and over 90% of the Center’s team members work directly in their communities. 
 For students interested in becoming more involved in Baltimore’s Indigenous community, the BAIC has a plethora of resources and events available. Gover Brooks emphasized this point in a statement. 
 “Students can get involved with the BAIC just by reaching out! You can sign up on our website to volunteer or reach out via e-mail or phone and ask us directly for more information. Most of our events are free to the community including our culture class which takes place at the center every Tuesday at 6:00pm-7:30pm. Please do not be a stranger, just show up if you have to & the center is happy to welcome any indigenous person looking to connect. Regardless of the background.” 
 The BAIC will be hosting a Native American Heritage Month celebration on Nov. 7, and it will also be hosting its annual Powwow on Nov. 21. 
 Students can also take a short shuttle ride downtown to Little Italy. They can see the site of the old Columbus Statue and then check out some of the great restaurants in the area. 
 “La Scala… it’s an Italian family that runs it. The best Italian restaurants are run by families… Benny’s is a good restaurant… and Chiapparelli’s got great pasta,“ Pica recommended. 
 Baltimore is a city with a complicated past. It is therefore no surprise that the city’s history of Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day is complex and dynamic, sure to change more in the coming years.
